Cardiology and hematology · published research

Blood properties

Experiments on isolated blood samples show that red and near-infrared light can alter red-cell flexibility, aggregation, and hemolysis, but responses vary by exposure. These laboratory findings do not show that treating people improves health.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Some sample experiments report improved red-cell behavior or reduced hemolysis under selected protocols, while other doses and settings show null or adverse changes. The human evidence concerns collected blood samples rather than patient treatment.

Summary of the Evidence

Recent experiments demonstrate both favorable and null blood responses. Stored human blood exposed to 589-nm light had less hemolysis during refrigeration than untreated samples, with smaller changes reported at 650 nm. Near-infrared studies of bovine red cells show that oxidative-stress responses depend on exposure level, and a 2026 equine platelet-product experiment found no change in the measured cytokines or growth factors (Mohammed et al. 2024; Walski et al. 2024; Max et al. 2026).

A 2022 narrative review discusses PBM effects on red-cell structure and function, including membrane behavior and deformability. It reports a broad literature synthesis but no pooled clinical effect estimate (Liebert et al. 2022).

Human and clinical evidence

No study in this indication treated patients to improve blood properties. Instead, human research irradiates blood after collection. A 2025 ex-vivo experiment exposed samples from ten adults to a 1-W, 810-nm high-power laser and reported changes in white-cell and red-cell indices. Those sample measurements do not show a health benefit or establish a treatment dose (Moghzi et al. 2025).

A 2026 equine experiment exposed platelet-rich plasma and autologous protein solution from six horses to a single high-intensity treatment. It found no significant change in the selected cytokines and growth factors, a null result for those products and markers (Max et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

Animal studies examine red-cell properties and blood handling in several models. In a porcine extracorporeal-circulation experiment, light exposure was associated with lower hemolysis markers and less red-cell lipid peroxidation, while red-cell count and hemoglobin did not differ from control (Walski et al. 2018).

In-vitro evidence

Experiments with isolated cells measure deformability, aggregation, viscosity, sedimentation, ATP, membrane structure, and oxidative stress. In isolated human red cells, 450-nm blue light at lower fluences improved deformability and weakened cell-cell interactions, while very high fluences increased aggregation and altered cell shape (Zhu et al. 2022).

In bovine red cells exposed to an oxidative stressor, near-infrared light showed a biphasic response. Lower-fluence protocols reduced hemolysis, while higher continuous exposure could increase cell-free hemoglobin. Pulsed exposure reduced hemolysis under some higher-dose conditions (Walski et al. 2024).

Ex-vivo evidence

Collected human blood irradiated at 589 nm showed a reported 23–42% reduction in hemolysis during refrigerated storage, compared with a 5–9% reduction after 650-nm exposure. The experiment followed stored aliquots for 21 days and addresses blood preservation rather than transfusion outcomes in patients (Mohammed et al. 2024).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols range from visible blue, yellow, and red light to near-infrared wavelengths. Exposure duration and fluence vary, and some experiments use high-intensity devices or unusual sample geometries. The dose-sensitive and sometimes opposing responses do not identify a validated wavelength or dose for treating people (Zhu et al. 2022; Walski et al. 2024; Moghzi et al. 2025).

Interpretation

The laboratory evidence shows that light can change blood-cell properties, including deformability and hemolysis, under specific exposures. Favorable, null, and adverse responses occur across different sample models and doses. Because the research uses collected blood or animal models, it provides very low certainty about any benefit from treating people.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low, primarily laboratory evidence. Laboratory and animal experiments report dose-sensitive biological effects, but no patient-treatment trial shows that a change in blood properties improves health.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

All directly relevant human experiments irradiate collected blood rather than treating patients. Results vary across samples and exposure protocols, and the animal and cell findings do not provide a clinical estimate. The single directly relevant synthesis is a narrative review of red-cell physiology, so certainty for a treatment benefit remains very low (Liebert et al. 2022; Walski et al. 2024).
